subject: Physics
title: Kabir's Auto-Rickshaw Ride: Newton's Laws Explained
hook: Why does a rickshaw suddenly jerk when the driver accelerates? Three laws of motion—Newton's gift to physics.

slides.title: Laws of Motion
slides.storyContext: Kabir and Ankita ride an auto-rickshaw through Delhi traffic. Driver Uncle explains motion without knowing Newton's laws—but physics is happening.

image.alt: Laws of Motion — Laws of Motion

slides.title: The Rickshaw Puzzle
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw is parked. Kabir asks Driver Uncle: 'Why doesn't the rickshaw move unless you accelerate it?' Driver Uncle scratches his head: 'That's just how it is.' Ankita jumps in: 'No, it's Newton! Things want to stay at rest. It's called inertia.' Kabir realizes: there's a law here.

image.alt: The Rickshaw Puzzle — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Newton's First Law: Inertia
slides.storyContext: Kabir sketches on paper: 'If no force acts on an object, it stays at rest or in motion forever. Inertia is resistance to change.'

points.label: The law
points.text: An object in motion stays in motion, and an object at rest stays at rest, unless acted upon by an external force.

points.label: Inertia
points.text: The natural tendency of an object to resist changes in motion. Mass is the measure of inertia.

points.label: Why the rickshaw jerks
points.text: When Driver Uncle suddenly accelerates, Kabir's body wants to stay at rest (inertia), so he feels pushed backward. When he brakes, he wants to keep moving forward.

points.label: Real-world examples
points.text: Passengers lurch when the train stops. Your phone slides on the car seat when the car turns. A coin falls straight down when you pull a tablecloth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Objects resist change. Once moving, they want to keep moving. At rest, they want to stay at rest. That's inertia.

image.alt: Newton's First Law: Inertia — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Why the Sudden Stop Hurts
slides.storyContext: Driver Uncle hits the brakes suddenly. Kabir lurches forward, his head nearly hitting the seat in front. Ankita laughs: 'See? Your body was moving. The rickshaw stopped, but you didn't—inertia is real!'

points.label: Your momentum
points.text: When moving, your body has momentum. When the rickshaw stops, friction acts on it but not on you (yet).

points.label: You continue straight
points.text: Your inertia makes you want to keep going forward—until you hit the seat, the seat exerts a force, and you stop.

points.label: Safety lesson
points.text: This is why seatbelts exist—to apply force gradually and stop you safely, spreading the deceleration over your whole body.

slides.inSimpleWords: Brakes slow the rickshaw, but your body wants to keep moving. That's Newton's first law: inertia resists the change.

image.alt: Why the Sudden Stop Hurts — Laws of Motion

slides.title: First Law Example: No External Force
slides.storyContext: A hockey puck is struck with initial velocity 5 m/s on perfectly smooth ice (no friction). Describe its motion.

example.problem: A hockey puck is struck with initial velocity 5 m/s on perfectly smooth ice (no friction). Describe its motion.
example.solution: Since there is no friction (no external force), the puck continues at 5 m/s indefinitely in a straight line. It doesn't slow down or change direction. By Newton's 1st law, v = constant when F = 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Without friction or other forces, moving things never slow down. They just keep going and going.

image.alt: First Law Example: No External Force — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Newton's Second Law: F = ma
slides.storyContext: Driver Uncle steps on the gas. Ankita asks: 'How hard he pushes matters, right?' Kabir replies: 'Yes! The engine's force determines the acceleration. That's F = ma.'

points.label: The law
points.text: Net force = mass × acceleration. F_net = ma. Force, mass, and acceleration are linked mathematically.

points.label: Force is a vector
points.text: 1 newton (N) is the force needed to accelerate 1 kg at 1 m/s². 1 N = 1 kg⋅m/s².

points.label: For the rickshaw
points.text: Engine produces force F. Rickshaw mass m ≈ 1000 kg. If F = 5000 N, then a = F/m = 5000/1000 = 5 m/s². Gentle acceleration.

points.label: Multiple forces
points.text: Net force = sum of all forces. If engine pushes with 5000 N and friction opposes with 2000 N, net F = 3000 N.

slides.inSimpleWords: Force causes acceleration. The more force, the more acceleration. The more massive the object, the less acceleration for the same force.

image.alt: Newton's Second Law: F = ma — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Why Lighter is Faster
slides.storyContext: Two rickshaws: one light (800 kg) and one heavy (1500 kg). Same engine force (5000 N). The light one accelerates faster. Kabir does the math: a_light = 5000/800 = 6.25 m/s², a_heavy = 5000/1500 = 3.33 m/s². He shouts: 'Same force, different mass, different acceleration!'

points.label: The physics
points.text: a = F/m. For fixed F, lighter objects accelerate faster. Mass in the denominator means inverse relationship.

points.label: In real life
points.text: Sports cars are light → they accelerate quickly. Trucks are heavy → they accelerate slowly. Same engine power has different effects.

points.label: Verification
points.text: Double the mass, halve the acceleration (for same F). This is Newton's second law predicting real behavior.

slides.inSimpleWords: Light objects accelerate more than heavy ones when pushed with the same force. F = ma means a = F/m—smaller m gives bigger a.

image.alt: Why Lighter is Faster — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Second Law Example: Rickshaw Acceleration
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw (m = 1200 kg) accelerates from rest with engine force 5000 N (ignoring friction). How fast is it after 3 seconds?

example.problem: Rickshaw: m = 1200 kg, F = 5000 N. Find acceleration and velocity after t = 3 s.
example.solution: Step 1: a = F/m = 5000/1200 ≈ 4.17 m/s². Step 2: Using v = u + at (with u = 0): v = 0 + 4.17 × 3 ≈ 12.5 m/s (about 45 km/h). The rickshaw reaches 45 km/h in 3 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: A 1200 kg rickshaw pushed by 5000 N accelerates at 4.17 m/s². After 3 seconds, it's moving at 12.5 m/s—that's real acceleration.

image.alt: Second Law Example: Rickshaw Acceleration — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Newton's Third Law: Action & Reaction
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw pushes forward on the road. Ankita asks: 'Does the road push back?' Kabir nods: 'Yes! The road pushes the rickshaw forward. That's Newton's third law.'

points.label: The law
points.text: For every action, there's an equal and opposite reaction. If A exerts force on B, then B exerts equal force on A (in opposite direction).

points.label: For the rickshaw
points.text: Wheels push backward on the road (action). Road pushes forward on wheels (reaction). This forward push accelerates the rickshaw.

points.label: Why both don't cancel
points.text: Action and reaction act on different objects (road and rickshaw). Newton's 2nd law applies separately to each.

points.label: Daily examples
points.text: Jump: you push Earth down, Earth pushes you up. Swim: push water backward, water pushes you forward. Throw: you push ball, ball pushes your hand.

slides.inSimpleWords: Forces always come in pairs. If you push on something, it pushes back with equal strength—just in the opposite direction.

image.alt: Newton's Third Law: Action & Reaction — Laws of Motion

slides.title: How the Rickshaw Actually Moves
slides.storyContext: Kabir realizes: 'The engine makes the wheels spin, but it's the road that actually propels us! The wheels push the road backward, and the road pushes us forward. We're using the Earth as a lever!' Driver Uncle laughs: 'Never thought of it that way, but yes—that's exactly it.'

points.label: Wheel-ground interaction
points.text: The wheels have friction with the road. Friction acts backward on the road (as the wheel tries to push backward).

points.label: Newton's 3rd law at work
points.text: By Newton's 3rd law, the road exerts friction forward on the wheels. This friction accelerates the rickshaw.

points.label: Why slippery roads fail
points.text: On ice, friction is reduced. Wheels can't grip, so they can't push the road backward with much force. The road can't push back much either. No acceleration.

slides.inSimpleWords: The rickshaw doesn't push itself forward. The wheels push the road, and the road pushes the rickshaw forward. They're a pair (Newton's 3rd law).

image.alt: How the Rickshaw Actually Moves — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Third Law Example: Jump
slides.storyContext: Kabir jumps from the rickshaw. His legs push the Earth downward with force F. By Newton's 3rd law, Earth pushes him upward with the same force F.

example.problem: Kabir (m = 60 kg) pushes downward on Earth with force 1200 N. By Newton's 3rd law, Earth pushes back with 1200 N upward. What's his acceleration during the jump?
example.solution: Step 1: Net force on Kabir = 1200 N (up) − 600 N (his weight, down) = 600 N up. Step 2: a = F_net / m = 600 / 60 = 10 m/s² upward. He accelerates upward at 10 m/s².

slides.inSimpleWords: When you jump, your legs push Earth down (action), and Earth pushes you up (reaction). Both forces are 1200 N, but they act on different objects (you and Earth).

image.alt: Third Law Example: Jump — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Types of Forces: Friction, Normal, Tension
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw slows down as traffic thickens. Kabir lists the forces: 'Brakes create friction. The seat holds us up (normal force). The rope tying luggage on top is under tension.'

points.label: Friction
points.text: Opposes motion. Kinetic friction f_k = μ_k × N (μ_k is coefficient, N is normal force). For the rickshaw: brakes create high friction.

points.label: Normal force
points.text: Perpendicular contact force. On level ground, N = mg (weight). The ground pushes up on Kabir with N = his weight.

points.label: Tension
points.text: Force in ropes/cables. A rope holding luggage is under tension T, pulling at both ends equally.

points.label: Weight
points.text: Gravitational force: W = mg (mass × gravity). Kabir's weight = 60 kg × 10 m/s² = 600 N downward.

slides.inSimpleWords: Friction slows things down. Normal force is the 'push' supporting weight. Tension is the 'pull' in ropes. Weight is gravity pulling down.

image.alt: Types of Forces: Friction, Normal, Tension — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Why Brakes Work (Friction's Glory)
slides.storyContext: Driver Uncle slams the brakes. Kabir feels the deceleration. Ankita asks: 'What force stops us?' Kabir laughs: 'Friction! The brake pads squeeze the wheels, friction acts opposite to motion, and we slow down. No friction, no stopping!'

points.label: Friction coefficient μ
points.text: Depends on surfaces: rubber on asphalt (μ ≈ 0.7−1.0), high friction. Ice on metal (μ ≈ 0.02), slippery.

points.label: Braking force
points.text: f = μ_k × N. If rickshaw presses brake pads with normal force N = 5000 N and μ_k = 0.8, friction f = 4000 N opposes motion.

points.label: Deceleration
points.text: a = −f/m = −4000/1200 ≈ −3.33 m/s² (negative: opposes motion). Strong braking!

slides.inSimpleWords: Friction is the force opposing motion. Brakes create high friction between pads and wheels. High friction = fast deceleration.

image.alt: Why Brakes Work (Friction's Glory) — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Applications: Inclines, Pulleys, and Elevators
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw climbs a slope toward a temple. Kabir realizes: 'The component of weight along the slope opposes motion. We're working against gravity.'

points.label: Inclined plane
points.text: Weight W = mg acts downward. Component parallel to slope: W_|| = mg sin(θ). Component perpendicular: W_⊥ = mg cos(θ). Friction opposes W_||.

points.label: For a 30° slope
points.text: W_|| = 100 kg × 10 × sin(30°) = 100 × 10 × 0.5 = 500 N pulling the rickshaw downhill.

points.label: Pulley systems
points.text: A rope over a pulley transmits tension. If mechanical advantage = 4, a 100 N pull lifts 400 N weight.

points.label: Elevator
points.text: When accelerating upward, normal force N > mg (you feel heavier). When accelerating downward, N < mg (lighter).

slides.inSimpleWords: On slopes, gravity has a component pulling downhill. Pulleys can amplify force. Elevators play tricks with normal force—making you feel heavier or lighter.

image.alt: Applications: Inclines, Pulleys, and Elevators — Laws of Motion

slides.title: The Temple Slope Challenge
slides.storyContext: Climbing the 30° slope to the temple, the rickshaw struggles. Kabir does the calculation: 'The component of gravity pulling downhill is 500 N per 100 kg. That's why it's harder!' Driver Uncle nods: 'Yep, low gear now. More torque, less speed.'

points.label: Force resolution
points.text: On a 30° slope, weight mg resolves into two components: one along the slope (mg sin 30°), one perpendicular (mg cos 30°).

points.label: Along-slope component
points.text: This component opposes upward motion. Larger θ means larger component. At θ = 90° (vertical), full weight opposes motion.

points.label: Equilibrium on slope
points.text: To move up at constant velocity, engine force must equal the along-slope component. Extra force is needed to accelerate uphill.

slides.inSimpleWords: Climbing a slope, part of gravity pulls you backward (down the slope). Steeper slope = stronger pull = harder to climb.

image.alt: The Temple Slope Challenge — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Incline Example: Force on a Slope
slides.storyContext: A 1000 kg rickshaw is on a 30° slope. Find the component of weight along the slope and perpendicular to it.

example.problem: Rickshaw (m = 1000 kg) on 30° slope. Find W_|| (along slope) and W_⊥ (perpendicular). Use g = 10 m/s².
example.solution: Step 1: Total weight W = mg = 1000 × 10 = 10,000 N downward. Step 2: W_|| = W sin(30°) = 10,000 × 0.5 = 5000 N (down the slope). Step 3: W_⊥ = W cos(30°) = 10,000 × 0.866 ≈ 8660 N (into the slope).

slides.inSimpleWords: On a 30° slope, a 10,000 N weight splits into 5000 N pulling downslope and 8660 N pressing into the slope.

image.alt: Incline Example: Force on a Slope — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Challenge: Tension in a Rope
slides.storyContext: A rope hangs from the ceiling with a weight hanging below. The rope's tension must support the weight. If the weight is accelerating upward, what is the tension?

example.problem: A 10 kg mass hangs from a rope. The rope pulls it upward with tension T. If the mass accelerates upward at 2 m/s², find T. (g = 10 m/s².)
example.solution: Step 1: Forces on mass: T (up) and weight W = mg = 100 N (down). Step 2: Net force F_net = T − W. Step 3: F_net = ma → T − 100 = 10 × 2 → T = 120 N. The tension must exceed the weight to accelerate it upward.

slides.inSimpleWords: A rope supporting a stationary weight has tension equal to the weight (100 N). If the weight accelerates upward, tension must be greater (120 N).

image.alt: Challenge: Tension in a Rope — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Worked Example: Rickshaw Braking
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw is moving at 10 m/s. Sudden red light! Driver Uncle brakes hard. Friction force f = 4000 N. Mass of rickshaw + passengers = 1200 kg. Find deceleration and stopping distance.

example.problem: A rickshaw (m = 1200 kg) moving at v = 10 m/s brakes with friction force f = 4000 N. Find deceleration and stopping distance.
example.solution: Step 1: Using F = ma, deceleration a = −F/m = −4000/1200 = −3.33 m/s² (negative because it opposes motion). Step 2: Using v² = u² + 2as (with final v = 0): 0 = 10² + 2(−3.33)s → s = 100/6.66 ≈ 15 meters. The rickshaw stops in 15 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Strong braking (4000 N force) on a heavy rickshaw (1200 kg) creates a deceleration of 3.33 m/s² and stops it in 15 meters—about the length of a bus.

image.alt: Worked Example: Rickshaw Braking — Laws of Motion

slides.title: Your Turn: Connected Masses
slides.storyContext: Two rickshaws are tied together (tension T in the rope). The first (m₁ = 1000 kg) is pulled by an engine with force F = 5000 N. The second (m₂ = 800 kg) is towed. Find acceleration and tension in the rope.

example.problem: Two connected masses: m₁ = 1000 kg (pulled by F = 5000 N), m₂ = 800 kg (towed). Find system acceleration and tension T in rope.
example.solution: Step 1: System acceleration a = F_total / m_total = 5000 / (1000 + 800) = 5000/1800 ≈ 2.78 m/s². Step 2: For the second rickshaw alone: T = m₂ × a = 800 × 2.78 ≈ 2222 N. The rope must pull with 2222 N to accelerate the second rickshaw.

slides.inSimpleWords: When masses are connected, they accelerate together. The tension in the connecting rope is just enough to pull the trailing mass.

image.alt: Your Turn: Connected Masses — Laws of Motion

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: The rickshaw reaches the destination safely. Driver Uncle smiles: 'All that math, and it's just driving!'

points.text: Newton's 1st Law: Objects resist change in motion (inertia). No net force = no acceleration.
Newton's 2nd Law: F_net = ma. Force causes acceleration. Bigger force = bigger acceleration (for same mass).
Newton's 3rd Law: Action and reaction are equal and opposite, acting on different objects.
Common forces: friction (opposes motion), normal force (supports weight), tension (pulls), weight (gravity).
On inclines, weight has components parallel and perpendicular to the slope.
For connected objects, find acceleration of the system, then use it for each object.

slides.inSimpleWords: Newton's laws connect force, mass, and acceleration. They explain why rickshaws jerk, why brakes work, why ropes tighten—everything moves according to these three laws.

image.alt: What You've Learned — Laws of Motion

subject: Physics
title: Maya's Farm: Why Work & Energy Matter
hook: A farmer pumps water uphill. The work done, energy stored, and power output tell the whole story.

slides.title: Work, Energy and Power
slides.storyContext: On a rural farm in Punjab, Maya helps her father pump water to irrigate the fields. A physics teacher visits and sees a lesson in energy.

image.alt: Work, Energy and Power — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: The Farmer's Wisdom
slides.storyContext: Father pumps water from a well 10 meters deep. Maya asks: 'Does it matter how fast you pump?' Father replies: 'Slower is less tiring, but takes longer.' The Teacher arrives and says: 'That's the difference between work and power. Work is done; power is the rate of doing work.'

image.alt: The Farmer's Wisdom — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Tired After Pumping
slides.storyContext: Maya pumps for an hour, lifting 500 kg of water 10 meters. She's exhausted but satisfied. Father says: 'You did 50 kilojoules of work. That's real effort.' The Teacher nods: 'Energy transferred from Maya to the water. That's what work means—moving energy from one place to another.'

points.label: Energy transfer
points.text: Work is the mechanism by which energy moves. Maya's muscles had energy; now the water has gravitational potential energy.

points.label: The calculation
points.text: W = mgh = 500 × 10 × 10 = 50,000 J = 50 kJ. This is how much energy was transferred.

slides.inSimpleWords: Work is energy moving from one place to another. Pumping water uphill takes energy from your muscles and stores it in the water's height.

image.alt: Tired After Pumping — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Work: Force & Displacement
slides.storyContext: The Teacher draws a diagram: 'Work is done when a force moves an object. But only the force component along the displacement counts.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Work W = F · s = F × s × cos(θ), where θ is the angle between force and displacement.

points.label: Unit
points.text: 1 joule (J) = 1 newton × 1 meter (N·m). 1 J is the work done by 1 N force over 1 m.

points.label: For the pump
points.text: Father lifts water mass m = 100 kg upward 10 m against gravity. Force = weight W = mg = 100 × 10 = 1000 N (downward). He applies F = 1000 N upward (opposite). Work = 1000 × 10 × cos(0°) = 10,000 J = 10 kJ.

points.label: No work if perpendicular
points.text: If force is perpendicular to motion (θ = 90°), cos(90°) = 0, so W = 0. Carrying a bucket horizontally does no work (gravity is perpendicular).

slides.inSimpleWords: Work is force times distance, but only the force in the direction of motion counts. Lifting upward does work against gravity; moving sideways at the same height does no work.

image.alt: Work: Force & Displacement — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Carrying Water Horizontally
slides.storyContext: Maya walks across the field carrying a full bucket of water. Father asks the Teacher: 'Is she doing work?' Teacher replies: 'The weight acts downward. Her motion is horizontal. Angle is 90°, so no work!' Maya laughs: 'But I'm tired!' Teacher explains: 'You're doing work against air resistance and friction in your joints, but the water's gravitational work is zero.'

points.label: Work = F · s · cos(θ)
points.text: F points down (gravity), s points horizontal. θ = 90°, cos(90°) = 0. So W = 0.

points.label: Why she's still tired
points.text: Her muscles do work against internal friction and air resistance, but the water doesn't gain height, so no gravitational work.

slides.inSimpleWords: Carrying a bucket horizontally does no work on the bucket's gravitational energy. Work only counts when force and motion are in the same direction.

image.alt: Carrying Water Horizontally — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Work Example: Lifting Water
slides.storyContext: Maya lifts a 20 kg bucket 1.5 meters. How much work does she do against gravity?

example.problem: Lifting 20 kg bucket 1.5 m against gravity (g = 10 m/s²). Find work done.
example.solution: Step 1: Force (weight) = mg = 20 × 10 = 200 N downward. Step 2: Displacement = 1.5 m upward. Step 3: Work W = F × s × cos(0°) = 200 × 1.5 × 1 = 300 J.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lifting a 20 kg bucket 1.5 meters requires overcoming 200 N of weight over that distance. That's 300 joules of work.

image.alt: Work Example: Lifting Water — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Energy: Kinetic & Potential
slides.storyContext: The Teacher explains: 'Energy is the capacity to do work. Two types: kinetic (motion) and potential (position).'

points.label: Kinetic energy KE
points.text: Energy of motion: KE = ½ m v². Unit: joules (J). If water flows at 2 m/s, KE = ½ × 100 × 2² = 200 J.

points.label: Gravitational potential energy PE
points.text: Energy of height: PE = mgh (relative to a reference). Water 10 m up: PE = 100 × 10 × 10 = 10,000 J.

points.label: Elastic potential energy
points.text: Energy stored in stretched springs: PE = ½ k x² (k = spring constant, x = compression/extension).

points.label: Total mechanical energy
points.text: E_total = KE + PE. At the top of the well, water has only PE. As it falls, PE converts to KE.

slides.inSimpleWords: Kinetic energy is energy of motion (KE = ½mv²). Potential energy is energy of height (PE = mgh). They can trade places: lift something high (gain PE), let it fall (PE → KE).

image.alt: Energy: Kinetic & Potential — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Water Falls and Speeds Up
slides.storyContext: Maya releases water from the raised tank. It falls 5 meters. Teacher asks: 'Where does its potential energy go?' Maya realizes: 'It speeds up! The PE becomes KE!'

points.label: At the top
points.text: 100 kg water at height 5 m: PE = 100 × 10 × 5 = 5000 J, speed v = 0 (at rest).

points.label: At the bottom
points.text: PE = 0 (height = 0), KE = ½ × 100 × v². If all PE → KE: 5000 = 50v² → v² = 100 → v = 10 m/s.

points.label: Energy conserved
points.text: Total E = 5000 J throughout the fall. It just changes form: PE → KE. In reality, some becomes heat (air resistance).

slides.inSimpleWords: Falling water loses height (PE) but gains speed (KE). The total energy stays the same, just changes form.

image.alt: Water Falls and Speeds Up — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Energy Example: Falling Water
slides.storyContext: 100 kg water falls from 10 m height. Find PE at the top and speed at the bottom (ignoring air resistance).

example.problem: 100 kg water at height h = 10 m. Find PE and speed when it reaches the ground (g = 10 m/s²).

slides.inSimpleWords: Water stored 10,000 joules of potential energy at 10 meters high. When it falls, all that energy becomes kinetic energy, reaching 14 m/s.

image.alt: Energy Example: Falling Water — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Conservation of Energy & Work-Energy Theorem
slides.storyContext: Maya watches water flow downhill from the raised tank. 'Where does the energy go?' The Teacher smiles: 'It's conserved—kinetic, potential, and heat from friction all add up to the work you did pumping.'

points.label: Energy conservation
points.text: Total mechanical energy = constant (no friction). KE + PE = constant. As height decreases, speed increases (PE → KE).

points.label: Work-energy theorem
points.text: Work done by net force = change in kinetic energy. W_net = ΔKE = ½m(v_f² − v_i²).

points.label: With friction
points.text: Work by all forces (including friction) = change in KE. W_applied − W_friction = ΔKE. Energy is lost as heat (thermal energy).

points.label: For the farm
points.text: Work pumped = 10 kJ. If no losses, this equals the water's PE at the top. In reality, friction in the pump wastes some energy as heat.

slides.inSimpleWords: Energy can't be created or destroyed, only changed form. Pumping adds energy; friction removes it. The net work determines change in kinetic energy.

image.alt: Conservation of Energy & Work-Energy Theorem — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Where Does the Energy Go?
slides.storyContext: Father notes: 'I pump 50 kJ, but the water only gains 50 kJ at the top. Good!' Teacher says: 'That's efficient pumping. In real pumps, some energy leaks as heat through friction in the pipes and pump bearings.'

points.label: Efficiency
points.text: Efficiency = (useful work out) / (work input) × 100%. A 90% efficient pump wastes 10% as heat.

points.label: Why friction matters
points.text: In the pipes, water rubbing against the walls creates friction. This friction force does negative work on the water (removes energy).

slides.inSimpleWords: Real pumps lose energy to friction. The efficiency tells you what fraction of the work input actually goes into lifting water versus wasted heat.

image.alt: Where Does the Energy Go? — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Power: Rate of Doing Work
slides.storyContext: Father pumps for 10 seconds. Maya asks: 'Does speed matter?' Teacher replies: 'Yes! Power is work per unit time.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Power P = Work / time = W / t. Unit: 1 watt (W) = 1 joule per second (J/s). 1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W.

points.label: For the pump
points.text: Work = 10,000 J. If pumped in 10 s, power P = 10,000 / 10 = 1000 W = 1 kW. If in 20 s, P = 500 W.

points.label: Instantaneous power
points.text: P = F · v = F × v × cos(θ). If force and velocity are in the same direction, P = F × v.

points.label: Real-world units
points.text: Electric bulb: 60 W (uses 60 J per second). Car engine: 50 kW. Heavy industry: megawatts (MW). Farm pump: typically 0.5−2 kW.

slides.inSimpleWords: Power is how fast work is done. 1 watt = 1 joule per second. A faster pump does the same work in less time, so higher power.

image.alt: Power: Rate of Doing Work — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Fast vs. Slow Pumping
slides.storyContext: Maya pumps slowly and steadily. Father says: 'Slow pumping is steady power.' She then speeds up frantically. Father: 'Fast pumping—you're increasing your power output!' Teacher notes: 'Same work if you pump the same total amount, but power differs by how fast you do it.'

points.label: Slow: 50 seconds
points.text: Work = 50 kJ, time = 50 s, power P = 50,000 / 50 = 1000 W.

points.label: Fast: 10 seconds
points.text: Work = 50 kJ, time = 10 s, power P = 50,000 / 10 = 5000 W.

points.label: Energy vs. power
points.text: Work (energy) is the same. Power is how fast it's delivered. Higher power = faster, more exhausting.

slides.inSimpleWords: Do 50 kJ of work in 10 seconds, and your power is high (5 kW). Do the same work in 50 seconds, and power is low (1 kW). Energy is conserved; power differs.

image.alt: Fast vs. Slow Pumping — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Power Example: Farm Pump
slides.storyContext: Father's pump lifts 200 kg water 10 m in 20 seconds. Find the work done and the power output.

example.problem: Pump lifts 200 kg water 10 m in 20 s. Find work and power. (g = 10 m/s².)

slides.inSimpleWords: Lifting 200 kg to 10 m height takes 20 kJ of work. If done in 20 seconds, the power is 1 kilowatt—a reasonable farm pump.

image.alt: Power Example: Farm Pump — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Collisions & Momentum (Bonus: Energy Perspective)
slides.storyContext: A stone falls into the tank. Water splashes. Teacher explains: 'In collisions, momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy might not be (some becomes heat, sound, deformation).'

points.label: Elastic collision
points.text: Both momentum and KE are conserved. Billiard balls bouncing: they rebound with minimal energy loss.

points.label: Inelastic collision
points.text: Momentum is conserved, but KE is not. Objects may stick together, and energy is lost as heat/deformation. Car crash: energy becomes crumpling metal and heat.

points.label: Perfectly inelastic
points.text: Objects stick together. Maximum KE loss (becomes internal energy). Example: mud hitting a wall.

slides.inSimpleWords: In collisions, momentum (mass × velocity) is always conserved. Kinetic energy might be lost (as heat, sound, deformation) in inelastic collisions.

image.alt: Collisions & Momentum (Bonus: Energy Perspective) — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Challenge: Kinetic Energy of Water
slides.storyContext: Water leaves the pump at 2 m/s. If 100 kg of water flows out each second, how much kinetic energy is transferred per second?

example.problem: 100 kg water leaves pump at v = 2 m/s. Find the kinetic energy per second (i.e., power output due to kinetic energy).
example.solution: Step 1: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 100 × 2² = ½ × 100 × 4 = 200 J per second. Step 2: Power = 200 J / 1 s = 200 W.

slides.inSimpleWords: Moving water carries kinetic energy. 100 kg at 2 m/s carries 200 joules. If this happens every second, the power is 200 watts.

image.alt: Challenge: Kinetic Energy of Water — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Worked Example: Lifting Water
slides.storyContext: Father pumps 1000 kg of water from a 15 m deep well in 30 seconds. Find work done, potential energy gained, and power.

example.problem: A pump lifts 1000 kg water from a 15 m deep well in 30 seconds. Find: (1) work done, (2) PE gained, (3) power.
example.solution: Step 1: Work against gravity W = mgh = 1000 × 10 × 15 = 150,000 J = 150 kJ. Step 2: PE gained = mgh = 150,000 J (same as work, assuming no friction). Step 3: Power P = W/t = 150,000 / 30 = 5000 W = 5 kW.

slides.inSimpleWords: Pumping 1000 kg up 15 meters requires 150 kilojoules of work. If done in 30 seconds, the power is 5 kilowatts—a substantial farm pump!

image.alt: Worked Example: Lifting Water — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: Your Turn: Spring Potential Energy
slides.storyContext: A farmer uses a spring-loaded water pump (spring constant k = 2000 N/m). He compresses the spring by 0.1 m and releases it to lift water. Find elastic PE and the water's speed if it gains that energy.

example.problem: Spring compressed by x = 0.1 m, k = 2000 N/m. Elastic PE is converted to water's KE. If water mass m = 0.5 kg, find final speed v.
example.solution: Step 1: Elastic PE = ½kx² = ½ × 2000 × (0.1)² = 1000 × 0.01 = 10 J. Step 2: By energy conservation, KE = PE, so ½mv² = 10 → v² = 20/0.5 = 40 → v = √40 ≈ 6.32 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compressing a spring by 0.1 m stores 10 joules. When released, that energy converts to kinetic energy, launching water at 6.3 m/s.

image.alt: Your Turn: Spring Potential Energy — Work, Energy and Power

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: Sunset on the farm. The tank is full, the crops are happy. Teacher smiles: 'You've done work, and the water has potential energy ready for tomorrow.'

points.text: Work W = F · s · cos(θ). Only the force component along displacement counts.
Kinetic energy KE = ½mv² (energy of motion). Potential energy PE = mgh (energy of height).
Energy is conserved: KE + PE = constant (without friction). With friction, some energy becomes heat.
Work-energy theorem: W_net = ΔKE. Net work equals change in kinetic energy.
Power P = Work / time (or P = F × v). Unit: watt (W) = joule per second.
In collisions, momentum is always conserved. KE might be lost (inelastic) or conserved (elastic).

slides.inSimpleWords: Work is force times distance. Energy is capacity to do work. Power is the rate. Conserve energy: what goes up must come down (or heat up).

image.alt: What You've Learned — Work, Energy and Power

subject: Physics
chapter: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
title: Ritesh's Spinning Top: Rigid Bodies & Angular Motion
hook: A top spins, never falling. But when you twist a stick, one end is faster than the other. Why? Rotation is different from translation.

slides.title: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
slides.storyContext: Ritesh spins a wooden top. It wobbles, rights itself, then spins steadily. Professor Anjali watches and begins a lesson about rotation.

image.alt: System of Particles and Rotational Motion — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: The Spinning Mystery
slides.storyContext: Ritesh notices: when the top spins fast, it's stable; when slow, it topples. Professor Anjali asks: 'Why does rotation stabilize it?' Priya joins: 'And how is rotation different from translation?' Ritesh realizes: rotation has its own physics, separate from linear motion.

image.alt: The Spinning Mystery — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Why the Top Doesn't Fall Over
slides.storyContext: The top wobbles when spinning slowly. Ritesh catches it and spins it faster. Now it's stable, barely wobbling. Professor asks: 'What changed?' Ritesh replies: 'It's spinning faster—higher angular velocity!' Professor: 'Yes, and that's angular momentum protecting it. The spin resists tipping.'

points.label: Precession
points.text: A wobbling top is precessing—its axis slowly rotates. Faster spin means less precession (more stable).

points.label: Angular momentum
points.text: L = Iω. A spinning top has large L. Changes to L require torque over time. Gravity tries to tip it, but high L resists.

slides.inSimpleWords: Spinning tops stay upright because angular momentum resists the force of gravity trying to tip them over. Faster spin = stronger resistance.

image.alt: Why the Top Doesn't Fall Over — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Angular Displacement, Velocity & Acceleration
slides.storyContext: Professor draws the top from above. 'Each point on the top moves in a circle. We describe this with angles, not distances.'

points.label: Angular displacement θ
points.text: Measured in radians (rad). Full circle = 2π rad ≈ 6.28 rad. (1 rad = 180°/π ≈ 57.3°.)

points.label: Angular velocity ω
points.text: Rate of angular change: ω = θ/t (radians per second, rad/s). Top spinning 10 rad/s is rotating fast.

points.label: Angular acceleration α
points.text: Rate of change of ω: α = Δω/Δt (rad/s²). Spinning up or slowing down.

points.label: Link to linear motion
points.text: For a point at radius r: linear velocity v = ωr; linear acceleration a = αr. Tip of the top moves faster than its center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Angular quantities (θ, ω, α) describe rotation like linear quantities (s, v, a) describe straight-line motion. Multiply by radius r to convert.

image.alt: Angular Displacement, Velocity & Acceleration — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Why the Tip Moves Faster
slides.storyContext: Ritesh marks the top with a pen at different radii: center, middle, edge. When spinning, the edge traces a bigger circle than the center, even though both rotate at the same angle per second. He calculates: 'Center at r = 0.5 cm, edge at r = 2 cm. Same ω = 50 rad/s. But v = ωr means v_center = 25 cm/s, v_edge = 100 cm/s. Four times faster!'

points.label: Same angular velocity
points.text: All points on the top rotate at the same ω (same angle per second).

points.label: Different linear velocity
points.text: v = ωr. Farther from axis = higher linear velocity. The tip spins much faster than the center.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotating objects have points moving at different linear speeds. The farther from the axis, the faster the linear motion (v = ωr).

image.alt: Why the Tip Moves Faster — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Angular Motion Example: Spinning Top
slides.storyContext: Ritesh's top completes 10 full rotations in 4 seconds. Find angular velocity and linear velocity at the edge (radius 2 cm).

example.problem: Top: 10 rotations in 4 s, edge radius r = 0.02 m. Find ω and v at edge.
example.solution: Step 1: 10 rotations = 10 × 2π = 20π rad. ω = 20π / 4 = 5π rad/s ≈ 15.7 rad/s. Step 2: v = ωr = 5π × 0.02 = 0.1π ≈ 0.314 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: A top spinning 10 times in 4 seconds has angular velocity 5π rad/s. The edge (2 cm away) moves at 0.31 m/s—quite fast for a toy!

image.alt: Angular Motion Example: Spinning Top — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Moment of Inertia: Rotational Mass
slides.storyContext: Professor spins a rod from its center, then from its edge. 'It's harder to spin from the edge—the mass is farther away. That's moment of inertia.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: I = Σ m_i r_i² (sum of mass × distance² for each part). Measures resistance to angular acceleration.

points.label: Unit
points.text: kg·m² (kilogram-meter squared).

points.label: Common shapes
points.text: Solid disk/cylinder: I = ½MR². Thin hoop: I = MR². Solid sphere: I = (2/5)MR². Long rod (about center): I = (1/12)ML².

points.label: For the top
points.text: If the top is approximated as a disk (M = 50 g, R = 2 cm), I = ½ × 0.05 × (0.02)² = 10⁻⁵ kg·m².

slides.inSimpleWords: Moment of inertia is how hard it is to spin something. Putting mass far from the axis increases I greatly (because of r²).

image.alt: Moment of Inertia: Rotational Mass — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Why the Hoop Spins Slower
slides.storyContext: Professor has two disks: one solid (disk), one a thin hoop (same mass and radius). She spins both. Priya notices: 'The hoop is harder to get spinning!' Professor: 'Yes. For a hoop, I = MR². For a disk, I = ½MR². The hoop has twice the I, so it needs twice the torque for the same angular acceleration.'

points.label: Hoop: I = MR²
points.text: All mass at radius R. Maximum moment of inertia.

points.label: Disk: I = ½MR²
points.text: Mass spread throughout, average distance smaller. Smaller I.

points.label: Physical meaning
points.text: The hoop is harder to spin because mass is far from axis. Concentration of mass at the edge increases rotational inertia.

slides.inSimpleWords: A hoop (mass at the edge) is harder to spin than a disk (mass throughout). r² in the formula means distance from the axis matters a lot.

image.alt: Why the Hoop Spins Slower — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Moment of Inertia Example
slides.storyContext: Compare a solid disk and a thin hoop, both M = 1 kg, R = 0.1 m. Find their moments of inertia.

example.problem: Disk and hoop: M = 1 kg, R = 0.1 m. Calculate I for each. Disk formula: I = ½MR². Hoop: I = MR².
example.solution: Step 1: Disk I = ½ × 1 × (0.1)² = 0.5 × 0.01 = 0.005 kg·m². Step 2: Hoop I = 1 × (0.1)² = 0.01 kg·m². The hoop's I is twice the disk's.

slides.inSimpleWords: A hoop has moment of inertia 0.01 kg·m², while a disk has 0.005 kg·m². The hoop is twice as hard to spin.

image.alt: Moment of Inertia Example — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Torque & Angular Momentum
slides.storyContext: Ritesh applies a force to the top's edge. Professor: 'The force's distance from the axis matters. That's torque—the rotational cousin of force.'

points.label: Torque τ
points.text: τ = r × F = r F sin(θ) (radius × force × sin of angle). Unit: N·m (newton-meter).

points.label: Newton's 2nd law (rotational)
points.text: τ = I α. Torque causes angular acceleration, like force causes linear acceleration.

points.label: Angular momentum L
points.text: L = I ω (inertia × angular velocity). Unit: kg·m²/s. A spinning top has large L.

points.label: Conservation
points.text: If no external torque acts, angular momentum is conserved. Spinning top: no external torque → L is constant → ω is constant (steady spin).

slides.inSimpleWords: Torque is rotational force. The farther from the axis you push, the more torque. Torque causes angular acceleration (τ = Iα). Angular momentum is conserved without external torque.

image.alt: Torque & Angular Momentum — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Why Leverage Matters
slides.storyContext: Ritesh tries to spin the top by pushing near the center (small r) versus near the edge (large r). Professor: 'Same force, but the edge push is more effective. That's because τ = r × F. Larger r means larger torque.'

points.label: Force near center
points.text: τ = F × 0.01 m (small r). Low torque.

points.label: Force near edge
points.text: τ = F × 0.05 m (large r). Five times more torque!

points.label: Practical lesson
points.text: Leverage in real life: a door handle is far from the hinge (large r) so you can open it easily. A hinge is close to the pivot (small r), so it holds firm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Torque depends on how far from the axis you push. Push far away → high torque → easy to spin. Push near the center → low torque → hard.

image.alt: Why Leverage Matters — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Torque Example: Spinning the Top
slides.storyContext: Ritesh applies 5 N force at the top's edge (r = 0.02 m, perpendicular to radius). Find the torque.

example.problem: Force F = 5 N applied perpendicular to radius r = 0.02 m. Find torque τ.

slides.inSimpleWords: A 5 N push at the edge (2 cm away) creates 0.1 N·m of torque. That's enough to start spinning a light top.

image.alt: Torque Example: Spinning the Top — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Rotational Kinetic Energy
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Does a spinning top have energy?' Professor: 'Yes! Rotational KE = ½Iω²—the spinning stores energy just like motion does.'

points.label: Rotational KE
points.text: KE_rot = ½Iω². Similar to linear KE = ½mv², but using I and ω instead of m and v.

points.label: For the top
points.text: I = 10⁻⁵ kg·m², ω = 100 rad/s (fast spin). KE = ½ × 10⁻⁵ × 100² = ½ × 10⁻⁵ × 10,000 = 0.05 J. Small but real.

points.label: Total mechanical energy
points.text: For a rotating object at height h: E_total = KE_linear + KE_rot + PE = ½mv² + ½Iω² + mgh.

points.label: Energy stored
points.text: A spinning flywheel stores rotational KE. Can be converted back to useful work (e.g., regenerative braking in trains).

slides.inSimpleWords: Spinning has kinetic energy just like moving does. A faster spin (larger ω) or larger moment of inertia (I) means more rotational energy.

image.alt: Rotational Kinetic Energy — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Rotational Energy Example: Spinning Top
slides.storyContext: The top spins at ω = 50 rad/s with I = 10⁻⁵ kg·m². Find its rotational kinetic energy.

example.problem: Top: I = 10⁻⁵ kg·m², ω = 50 rad/s. Find KE_rot.

slides.inSimpleWords: A spinning top stores about 12.5 millijoules of energy. When friction slows it down, this energy dissipates as heat.

image.alt: Rotational Energy Example: Spinning Top — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Rolling Without Slipping: Combined Motion
slides.storyContext: A ball rolls down an incline. Priya asks: 'Is it just rotating, or is it also translating?' Professor: 'Both! And there's a constraint: rolling without slipping means v = ωr.'

points.label: Rolling condition
points.text: For no slipping: v_center = ωr (linear velocity of center = angular velocity × radius).

points.label: Total KE
points.text: KE_total = ½mv_center² + ½Iω² = ½mv² + ½I(v/r)². This is split between translation and rotation.

points.label: For a solid sphere
points.text: I = (2/5)mr². So KE = ½mv² + ½(2/5)mr²(v/r)² = ½mv² + (1/5)mv² = (7/10)mv². 70% goes to translation, 30% to rotation.

points.label: Down an incline
points.text: A solid sphere accelerates slower than a sliding block (friction-free) because energy goes into rotation. v_sphere² = (10/7)gh (at bottom), v_block² = 2gh.

slides.inSimpleWords: A rolling ball has two kinds of motion: its center moves forward (translation) and the ball spins (rotation). No slipping means v = ωr.

image.alt: Rolling Without Slipping: Combined Motion — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: A Ball Rolling Down the Temple Slope
slides.storyContext: Ritesh rolls a ball down the slope. Priya asks: 'Will it slide or roll?' Professor: 'With friction, it rolls. Friction prevents slipping but still exerts a torque, spinning the ball.' Ritesh calculates: 'So some energy goes into rotation, and it reaches the bottom slower than if it slid?'

points.label: With friction
points.text: Friction acts backward on the ball's contact point (opposes sliding). This friction acts at a distance r from the center, creating torque.

points.label: Rolling constraint
points.text: The friction keeps v = ωr. The ball rolls without slipping.

points.label: Energy split
points.text: Potential energy converts to both translational and rotational KE. This is why rolling is slower than sliding.

slides.inSimpleWords: Friction makes a ball roll instead of slide. Rolling splits energy between forward motion and spinning, so the ball reaches the bottom slower.

image.alt: A Ball Rolling Down the Temple Slope — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Worked Example: Spinning Top
slides.storyContext: Ritesh spins the top with initial ω = 50 rad/s. Air resistance and friction create a torque τ = −0.001 N·m. If I = 10⁻⁵ kg·m², how long until the top stops?

example.problem: Top: I = 10⁻⁵ kg·m², ω_initial = 50 rad/s, torque τ = −0.001 N·m (due to friction). Find time to stop.
example.solution: Step 1: Angular acceleration α = τ/I = −0.001 / 10⁻⁵ = −100 rad/s². Step 2: Using ω_f = ω_i + αt (with ω_f = 0): 0 = 50 + (−100)t → t = 0.5 s. The top stops in half a second.

slides.inSimpleWords: Friction torque causes the top to decelerate. Angular acceleration = torque/moment of inertia. A small top stops quickly because friction's torque is comparable to its small inertia.

image.alt: Worked Example: Spinning Top — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Challenge: Angular Momentum Conservation
slides.storyContext: An ice skater spins with arms extended (I = 5 kg·m², ω = 2 rad/s). She pulls her arms in, reducing I to 2 kg·m². Find her new angular velocity. (No external torque.)

example.problem: Skater: initial I_1 = 5 kg·m², ω_1 = 2 rad/s. Final I_2 = 2 kg·m². Find ω_2 using L_1 = L_2.
example.solution: Step 1: Initial angular momentum L = I_1 ω_1 = 5 × 2 = 10 kg·m²/s. Step 2: Final: L = I_2 ω_2 = 2 × ω_2. Step 3: 10 = 2 × ω_2 → ω_2 = 5 rad/s. She spins 2.5 times faster!

slides.inSimpleWords: When a spinning skater pulls her arms in, her moment of inertia decreases, so her angular velocity must increase (to conserve L). She spins faster.

image.alt: Challenge: Angular Momentum Conservation — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: Your Turn: Rolling Sphere
slides.storyContext: A solid sphere (mass m = 2 kg, radius r = 0.1 m) rolls down a frictionless 5 m incline (angle 30°). Find final linear velocity at the bottom.

example.problem: Sphere (m = 2 kg, r = 0.1 m) rolls down a frictionless 5 m incline (30° angle). Find v at the bottom. (I_sphere = (2/5)mr².)
example.solution: Step 1: Potential energy PE = mgh = mg(L sin θ) = 2 × 10 × 5 × sin(30°) = 2 × 10 × 5 × 0.5 = 50 J. Step 2: At the bottom, this converts to KE. For rolling: KE = (7/10)mv² = 50 J → v² = 50 × 10 / (7 × 2) = 500/14 ≈ 35.7 → v ≈ 5.98 m/s ≈ 6 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: A sphere rolling down 5 meters loses 50 joules of potential energy. Part becomes translational KE, part becomes rotational KE. Final speed is about 6 m/s.

image.alt: Your Turn: Rolling Sphere — System of Particles and Rotational Motion

slides.title: What You've Learned
slides.storyContext: The top wobbles to a stop. Ritesh sweeps it off the table. Professor smiles: 'You've seen the full dance—translation and rotation, inertia and torque, energy and momentum.'

points.text: Angular displacement (θ), velocity (ω), and acceleration (α) describe rotation. Related to linear by radius: v = ωr, a = αr.
Moment of inertia I = Σm_ir_i² measures resistance to angular acceleration. I depends on shape and axis.
Torque τ = rF sin(θ) causes angular acceleration: τ = Iα. Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved without external torque.
Rotational kinetic energy KE_rot = ½Iω². Total energy mixes translation, rotation, and potential.
Rolling without slipping: v = ωr. Energy splits between translational and rotational KE.
Center of mass motion (system of particles) follows ΣF_ext = M·a_cm (independent of internal forces).

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotation is a parallel world to translation. Moment of inertia (I) is like mass, torque (τ) is like force, angular momentum (L) is like linear momentum. Conserve energy and momentum.

image.alt: What You've Learned — System of Particles and Rotational Motion
